implementation_notes: The JDK ships the vocabulary the catalog names: `Function.andThen`/`compose`, `Predicate.and`/`or`/`negate`, `UnaryOperator.identity`, `Comparator.thenComparing`, `Optional.map`/`flatMap`/`or`, and `Stream.map`/`filter`/`flatMap`/`reduce`. A domain DSL is built from these interfaces (or from one small custom functional interface with default methods), which retires hand-written Strategy objects. The classic hierarchy is still justified when combinators must be introspected (annotation processors, serialisation) or when the DSL is implemented by many teams behind a stable interface plus factory.
pitfalls: `andThen` and `compose` run in opposite directions; when the value types coincide a mis-ordered chain type-checks and silently runs backwards.
Lambdas cannot throw checked exceptions: putting I/O or reflection inside a `Function` forces wrapper types, `UncheckedIOException` noise, or a custom throwing interface.
Streams are single-use: storing a stream in a field and re-consuming it throws IllegalStateException - share the combinator, not the stream.

variants.name: Vavr persistent collections and control structures
variants.implementation_notes: Vavr supplies what the JDK lacks for a pure combinator library: persistent (immutable) collections and monadic control structures - `Option`, `Try`, `Either`, `Validation` - each with `map`/`flatMap`/`fold`/`getOrElse` combinators and conversions to the JDK types. Choose it when the DSL's values are themselves the domain (error accumulation, effect descriptions, immutable state) and referential transparency matters; keep the JDK variant when only collection transformation is needed, since Vavr adds a dependency and its collections do not implement the JDK collection interfaces.
pitfalls: Vavr collections are not JDK collections: without explicit conversion (`toJavaList` and friends) framework and serialization code breaks at the boundary.
Mixing JDK `Optional` and Vavr `Option` (or `Try` inside an `Either` flow) is a classic confusion: pick one inside the DSL and convert at the edges.
Persistent data structures trade copying for sharing; write-heavy loops and per-step `getOrElse`-style combinators allocate more than a mutable alternative.
